title: Shortest Maze Path
statement:
A maze is a grid where `0` is an open cell and `1` is a wall. You start at the top-left cell and want to reach the bottom-right cell. In one move you can step **up, down, left or right** into an open cell (never into a wall, never outside the grid).

Return the **fewest moves** needed. If it is impossible (including when the start or the end is a wall), return `-1`. If the grid is a single open cell, the answer is `0`.
constraints: 1 <= rows, cols <= 100 (every row has the same length)

examples.explanation: Both neighbours of the start are walls.

hints.nudge: All moves cost the same. If you explore outward from the start one step at a time, when will you first reach each cell?
hints.pseudocode:
if start or end is a wall: return -1
queue = [(0, 0)]; dist[0][0] = 0
while queue not empty:
  (r, c) = pop front
  if (r, c) is the end: return dist[r][c]
  for each open unvisited neighbour: dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1; push it
return -1
hints.walkthrough: Trying every path (depth-first with backtracking) is exponential. Because every move costs 1, a breadth-first search visits cells in order of distance from the start: first all cells 1 move away, then 2 moves away, and so on. So the first time BFS reaches the end cell, that distance is the minimum. Use a queue, a visited marker (or distance table) so no cell is queued twice, and check the four neighbours. If the queue empties without reaching the end, return -1. O(rows * cols) time.
